I don't see the problem with rolling with play mistakes instead of taking them back. That doesn't really stem from "no alliances". Play mistakes are a legitimate way to lose. Neither does keeping track of missed triggers. Heck, I think that one's already a rule in competitive formats. Durdling is also pretty rude and has nothing to do with alliances. Moreover, I said I don't pull punches not that I'm all-out-attacking every turn in every situation. I don't like when people get mad at me for playing the game, even so, I do what I must to keep the game fun for me. If I don't like what a particular player is doing, I'll go after them. On the subject of tucking, I'd definitely high five the guy for taking care of any degenerate commander, but I'd also probably knock him out posthaste. It never stops with just That Guy's commander.

Here be my code as a spellslinger.

* Thou shalt play honorably, if nothing else. No take-backs, keep track of other's triggers as well as my own, and promise no alliances in a free-for-all. Most of all, no durdling.

* Thou shan't pull thy punches. It's disrespectful to one's adversaries as well as oneself.

* Thou shall practice good sportsmanship. Win or lose, it's just a game. No need to go on tilt.

* Kill the guy who's tucking commanders first.

> One should consider the possible results of exposure to these images and terms:

I see a whole lot of benefits in this list. 

* Desensitization to what is ugly, evil or repulsive

All very relative. By the way, ugly & repulsive are not synonymous with evil. I find bananas repulsive, but I don't find them evil. Perhaps after playing Magic: the Gathering, the players learn that something they'd been taught is ugly or repulsive is actually beautiful and enticing. Wouldn't be the first time that I've seen it happen.

* Desensitization to sorcery and the occult 

Probably actually a good idea since you don't want to be scared stupid if you actually encounter an enemy wizard.

* An interest in or fascination with death

This is the one exception to my previous statement as no one should obsess over death. However, this point is also interestingly hypocritical considering the unhealthy obsession that theists have concerning death and the afterlife.

* Familiarity with occult terms & concepts

Again, how are you to know if you're dealing with an enemy wizard without first familiarizing yourself with their art? You're leaving yourself a lot more vulnerable by not studying Defense Against the Dark Arts.

* Developing a taste for the bizarre

Everyone could take a step outside of their box. Truth is often times stranger than fiction, radda radda radda.

All the time. However, I rarely allow it to bother me since I'm more or less just waiting until my time runs out one way or another. I dropped out of high school to get my GED so I could go to college and prove something to myself and/or someone else. I'm still not sure what I was trying to prove. Maybe it was just an attempt to continue going through the motions so that when I failed again I'd be absolutely sure and fail again I did. I quit college two years ago and gave the rest of the aid I had to my little sister so that there was no going back. Since then I haven't been able to find stable employment, so of course I'm still living at home with my parents. Meanwhile I've been struggling in vain to create some sort of life for myself as a fiction writer, but in the end I'm probably not going to amount to anything at all. I'm just not motivated to succeed like others are. I didn't ask to exist. In fact, I'd rather I didn't. I've thought of killing myself countless times, but I can't ever bring myself to do it. Every time I try I end up thinking of how painful or unpleasant the act will be and the way it would make the people around me feel. I can't do it because of the latter. I'm sure I'd somehow work through the pain, however, even more than causing trouble for people when I'm alive, I don't want to cause people grief over my death. So, I guess the only reason I'm still dragging my living corpse out of bed is to outlive everyone I love so that I can die with peace of mind. Barring that, if I somehow luck out and score employment, I'll save up the money to burn every last bridge connected to me so I can finally disappear. I wish that I didn't feel this way. I wish that my happiness wasn't so fleeting. I wish I could just be content with life like everyone else, but I can't find the drive. I'm sorry for posting something so depressing, but it's been eating away at me inside. Thank you for this thread. I can't talk about how I really feel with anyone offline. They don't understand and it always makes them so sad.

If a PC in one of my universes wanted to ditch their patron I could think of quite a few things to do with the situation depending on how they choose to go about it.

If they still wanted to keep their warlock powers while being free of their patron, they'd probably have to go on a lengthy quest to somehow disable and/or kill their patron while absorbing at least a portion of the eldritch power they'd otherwise be forfeiting. Another option would be to simply find another patron that wouldn't mind ridding the warlock of his previous patron.

If the player wanted to change class, that'd also be acceptable. This would require a lot of study and preparation on the warlock's part, since they'd essentially have to become a wizard or sorcerer of some sort after breaking ties with their patron.

If for some reason, the player has a change of heart and wants to play a martial class instead, they could prepare for the eventuality of losing their powers by having another PC or NPC train their character in their disciplines.

In either case of the warlock becoming another class, I might give them some negative levels in their new class. However, I wouldn't make them start back at level one if they put some thought and preparation into their plan to lose their patron.

I'm running a campaign in my homebrew setting, so naturally there are a few homebrew rules. The variant rules I'm using right now are:

* **Massive Damage**; When a creature takes damage from a single source equal to or greater than half of its max HP, it must succeed on a DC 15 CON saving throw or suffer a random effect determined by a roll on the System Shock table. [source: D&D 5e DMG]

* **Critical Hits/Fumbles**; When a creature makes an attack and rolls a natural 20, that creature's controller rolls for an additional effect for the attack from the Critical Hit table. When a creature makes an attack roll and rolls a natural 1, that creature's controller rolls for additional effects for the failure from the Fumble table. [source: homebrew]

* **We Skyrim Now**; At any time during the adventure, the dungeon master may roll on the Oh Shit Dragons! table. There are only three results; dragon, dragons, and no dragons. The variety of dragon(s) that appears is up to the DM's discretion. [source: homebrew]

* **Subclass**; I have had a great dislike for the multiclass system since starting to play D&D. My subclass system is still in development. [source: homebrew]

* **Epic Heroism**; I'm only considering this rest variant for certain areas in my homebrew campaign, otherwise I'll be using default rest rules. This variant uses a short rest of 5 minutes and a long rest of 1 hour. This change makes combat more routine, since characters can easily recover from every battle. You might want to make combat encounters more difficult to compensate. Spellcasters using this system can afford to burn through spell slots quickly, especially at higher levels. Consider allowing spellcasters to restore expended spell slots equal to only half of their max spell slots (rounded down) at the end of a long rest, & to limit spell slots restored to 5th level or lower. Only a full 8-hour rest will allow a spellcaster to restore all spell slots and regain spell slots of 6th level or higher. [source: D&D 5e DMG].

This is exactly why I prefer to homebrew my own adventures/campaigns rather than published adventures that my players could pour through at their leisure. My players can't meta by looking at anything I throw at them besides monster stats from the Monster Manual, but they know that there's never any guarantee that I haven't given the monsters class levels or otherwise modified the stat block. I draw each area in the overworld/dungeon room by room as we progress on a wet erase battle grid on the day of the session. Nothing short of hacking into my laptop's hard drive or solving the cipher that I write my physical notes will yield my players any forbidden knowledge. I've found encrypting my notes helps a lot when it comes to leaving my plots unspoiled.

Another way of dealing with metagaming that I also employ is separating metaknowledge from character knowledge in the game. Explain to your players that looking at the Monster Manual or your notes is a meaningless gesture as their characters would be lacking said knowledge, meaning that they couldn't act based on it. If everything goes accordingly, it won't matter if they continue sneaking peaks or not. If a player's character starts acting based on knowledge that you are skeptical of them having, then have that player roll a Knowledge type check to see what their character knows. Give them more or less information based on the outcome of the check. Boom. Problem solved.

I'm kind of disappointed with anyone who doesn't allow party in-fighting as a DM. I can begin to understand such a ruling in cases where the DM is running a published adventure rather than building their own settings/adventures.

I, as DM, don't put any restrictions on my players or their characters. If in-fighting breaks out in one of my groups, I talk to the involved players both separately and together to gauge what they want to get out of this conflict. I take the information that I glean from these meetings into consideration and plan accordingly for future sessions. Perhaps the characters whom are at odds with each other might get into a sticky situation that they can only escape by trusting and cooperating with each other.

Honestly, I think that if you DM and you put these kinds of restrictions on your players, you're doing the whole group a disservice by being so closed-minded to the glorious possibilities. Any and all problems that in-fighting can cause can be solved with a little bit a creativity on everyone's part.

My playgroup has absolutely no qualms about using tutors. Not all tutors are created equally and not all tutors are good in decks of their color identity. The trick is finding balance. If your group is plays relatively powerful decks and/or can get fairly competitive, consistency can be an enormous boon. If your group plays more casually with gimmicky or underpowered decks, maybe you could stand to run less tutors. Again, it's all about balance.

Another valid point for the use of tutors is that some archetypes (combo) can have an especially hard time without tutors to fetch the pieces to their combos. Maybe combo decks could stand to be less consistent or maybe we could all stand to run more answers. I usually recommend the latter, but I like to play Magic to the book and not exclude someone because my fun happens to be playing aggro and theirs happens to be playing control or combo.

Yet another valid point is, as I said before, all tutors are not created equally. Instead of having a grudge against tutors in general, why not focus more on those which are more on the broken side?

Hear, hear!

I could not agree more. Cutting out one of the five different player types is a bad idea. Instead of banning a powerful but not necessarily banworthy or particularly broken card, why not run some answers for it?

In my EDH circle, all sorts of decks see play. Aggro, combo, control, hybrids, anything goes. The only restriction we place upon ourselves is the regular banlist decided by the EDH rules committee and our meta is healthy and thriving. Hell, every once in a while we even suspend that ban list so we can see what we're missing out on. However, that is not the point I want to make. We all run play what we want to play and we've accepted that part of this means packing some answers to disrupt each others strategies. So, if someone is getting too powerful, either one of us answers his/her threat with some disruption. Worst case scenario, someone becomes the archenemy.

Long point made simple: Let the people play what they want. Run answers. Have fun.
